subject: strandbeest
pitch:
Category: Abstract.
Subject: wind-walking beach creature of tubes.
Style: Theo Jansen kinetic sculpture.
reasoning:
I'm envisioning a Strandbeest-style creature built as a module with an SDK—PVC tube legs using Jansen linkages, sail-like wings, walking on a beach. I'm sketching rough dimensions, aiming for something around 3.2m long and 2m wide, balancing scale with craftsmanship and efficiency.

I'm settling on a color palette (yellow tubes, white sail fabric, blue-gray zip ties, dark pivot bolts) and planning the frame structure—two triangulated side trusses with a shared crankshaft driving multiple Jansen leg mechanisms offset in phase, using the classic Jansen linkage proportions scaled to fit.

Working out the circle-intersection geometry for each leg joint...

I don't trust these distances enough to verify by hand, so I'll make the math robust at runtime by clamping values to avoid NaN and adding a fallback foot position, then offset the leg pivots so the foot's lowest point across the walking cycle lands near ground level.

For resting pose, I want all legs touching the floor at their lowest point, so I'll compute joint positions for each leg, find the global minimum foot height across all legs, and shift the whole body up by that offset. I'm now working through the Jansen linkage's standard coordinates, starting with the fixed pivot and crank axle, then building out each connected joint in sequence.

Mapping out the linkage lengths and connections between joints to figure out the full triangle chain.

Still figuring out the remaining joint distances and triangle sides for P5 and P6, trying rough estimates for the foot triangle before settling on how to pick the intersection side.

I'll handle the sign ambiguity by choosing whichever solution keeps the foot below P4 for a sensible walking shape, testing the setup at θ=0 with the fixed points to sanity-check the distances work out numerically.

Trying to decide whether P2 goes up and P3 down to form the kite shape, then checking if the resulting P4 and P5 distances stay consistent with the bar lengths before placing P4 on the outward side.

Now I'm working through P5 and P6 positions using the triangle distance constraints from P2 and P4, checking which side of each line the points should fall on to match the mechanism's geometry, settling on P4 to the left and P6 below P5 outward from the linkage.

I'm picking a scale factor so leg lengths translate to roughly a meter of height, keeping the overall body-to-frame proportions sensible. For the leg arrangement, I'm spacing multiple leg units per side across different crank phases and x offsets so they interleave along the z-axis the way real Jansen-linkage walkers do.

Each leg needs 11 rod bars plus joint bolts, totaling roughly 140 parts across all 8 legs. I'm planning joint hierarchy for rigging, giving each leg a crank axle joint to drive the chain of moving parts.

Working out joint coordinates...

Now I'm laying out the frame structure: crankshaft and pivot rods spanning the width, triangular trusses on each side connecting to upright supports, a ridge beam and cross braces on top, plus a spine beam. I'm also considering adding wind-catching sails inspired by Jansen's design, using a fabric panel toward the rear.

Writing sail paint textures...

I'm aiming for around 300 lines covering 180+ parts, skipping any ground or beach elements since the pitch doesn't call for them, though I might add small sandal-like foot plates. I'm defining the color palette next: a mottled yellow PVC with scuffs, dark bolts, blue zip ties, and an off-white sail fabric.

Now I'm working out the crank mechanism geometry and leg trajectories, computing each leg's position in 3D space based on phase offsets, then finding the minimum foot height across all legs so I can set the body's vertical offset for proper floor contact, accounting for shoe thickness at each foot.

I'm defining the joint hierarchy next, chaining hip-knee-foot joints as a leg under the body joint, attaching foot contact points, and setting up rotating crank joints per leg anchored at point A along the x-axis direction.

Now I'm adding the crank arm with its pin, assigning the connecting rods between C and the knee bars, and building a rod helper that draws cylindrical bars with bolts at each pivot point, offsetting each leg's bars slightly in x so the stacked planes don't collide.

I'm also laying out the frame geometry per side—defining top beam height, outer post positions, and the front/back truss points—then connecting them with rods to form a triangulated support structure.

For the legs, I need to figure out the z-range they sweep through so I can center the pivot point: I'll compute the average foot position over a full gait cycle at zO=0, then shift zO by the negative of that average so the feet stay roughly centered at z≈0.

Now I'm adding the structural cross beams connecting Fr/Bk and Ps/Ac, plus a center spine. I'm also planning a front wind-vane nose, a rear mast with a triangular sail, a smaller front jib, and a row of cylindrical bottles along the top of the frame.

I'm building bottle geometry with cylinder bodies, cone shoulders, and caps, plus small zip-tie boxes and short collar cylinders at beam joints to simulate couplings.

For the sails, I'm designing an SVG texture with off-white fabric, seam lines, faded teal panels, and stitching detail, using alpha transparency to cut a triangular sail shape out of a flat plane, with front and back layers for double-sided visibility.

I'll go with trapezoidal sails with scalloped tops, mounted on vertical masts placed along the spine at three positions, facing outward like fins. I'm also considering adding a simple head or eye detail near the front to give the creature more character.

Writing geometry helpers...

Working through the geometry, I compute P5 by finding the intersection point using perpendicular offsets from the P2-P4 baseline, landing up-left near (-23.8, 28); then I move to solving for P6 using the distances from P4 and P5, picking the minimum option along the perpendicular direction.

But something's off — the computed P6 ends up with a positive y-coordinate above the pivot, which doesn't match the real Jansen linkage foot, which should sit well below the pivot. This tells me I've mislabeled which vertex is the actual foot joint, so I need to reassign which point represents the kite's lower vertex.

Trying the other candidate side also lands far from the expected bottom position, so I'm starting to think my P2/P3 assignment itself is flawed — these two points shouldn't be as far apart as I've placed them. I should go back to the actual Jansen leg diagram layout starting from the top pivot to get the geometry right.

Still working through the triangulation for P5 and P6, trying to place the foot joint using distances from P3 and P4 with the law of cosines, solving for the intersection coordinates numerically.

Taking the correct sign gives P6 at (15.4, -66.2), the lowest point, matching a plausible foot-swing extending below the pivot — total leg height scales to about 0.9 m, which seems reasonable for a gait-like linkage. I'll accept this and move on to listing the bar connections: O-P2, O-P3, C-P2, C-P3, P2-P4, P3-P4, and so on.

For other θ values, picking candidates could flip inconsistently since min/max selection isn't stable across rotations, so I need to anchor choices by continuity rather than absolute rules — defining a reference solution at θ=0 and then picking whichever candidate at other angles stays closest to that reference to avoid discontinuous jumps.

I'll clamp leg height to zero when the circles don't intersect, and compute the floor as the minimum foot height across all four gait phases, using phase offsets between left and right sides for a natural walking variation.

Now I'm setting up the color palette for the model -- defining paint shades for the hull, dark trim, zippers, bottle, cap, sails, and rope -- and working out the coordinate transform so each leg's foot position maps correctly into world space with the body centered at the mean rest position.

Next I'm structuring the build process: creating the builder object, then computing leg joint geometry for each side and phase offset before constructing the body, leg chains, frame, and bolts. I'm precomputing the vertical offset so the lowest foot point rests just above the ground, accounting for a small shoe thickness.

Then for each leg I'm mapping its points to 3D vectors scaled by side and x-offset, building a named joint chain (hip, knee, foot) per leg with unique tags for left/right, and setting up the crank joint that drives the leg motion.

Adding rod/tube helpers and bolt parts...

Still working out the frame geometry...

I'm also planning to add a center top beam with struts, plus rows of bottle-shaped cylinders arranged along the top at alternating x positions, roughly a dozen per side with alternating cap colors.

Each bottle needs a lathed shoulder/neck profile for realism, with a separate small cap piece, so two parts per bottle. I'm also figuring out where to add supporting crossbars underneath so the bottles rest properly on the frame rather than floating over gaps.

Now I'm planning the mast and sail setup rising from the center beam, with vertical masts and thin sail planes positioned on either side, checking that the plane orientations face correctly so the sails read as upright rectangles.

For the sail texture I'm drafting an SVG trapezoid shape with cream fills, panel seams, hem stitching, corner grommets, and a teal wave motif near the bottom, all clipped to the sail outline. Now I'm thinking about placing eye spheres on the front crossbeam so they sit facing forward.

For the eyes, I'm mounting two small eye discs on stalks above the front crossbar, using white spheres with flat circular pupil textures positioned just inside the sphere surface so they appear coplanar with the curved front.

Adding a shoe box for the foot and considering a tennis-ball weight. For textures, I'll use paint functions on the lathe bottle to add a label band based on height, and a similar paint gradient for sand near the shoe's bottom rather than separate texture maps.

Now I'm setting up randomness for bottle color variety and sail tilt, then drafting the leg geometry using a two-circle intersection function to compute joint positions from fixed anchor points.

Still computing leg points...

Now I'm planning the full code structure: setting rod radii for bars, frame, and crankshaft, then building limb chains with joints named by hip/knee/foot and assigning which points connect to the hip versus knee for each leg.

Mapping which bolts and pins belong at each point (O, C, P2-P6) per leg gives roughly 144 bolts, 88 rod connections, plus shoes and crank pins — tallying up to around 330 total components, well under my limit. I'm also adding small details like disc end caps on the axle and simple eye textures before writing the final frame rod layout.
